Here are the coolest e-motorcycles and gear we saw at EICMA 2026

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2047 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that every year, the world’s largest motorcycle companies (and plenty of the world’s smallest motorcycle companies, too) converge on Milan, Italy for Europe’s premier motorcycle showcase.
  • Below is a list of the best things I saw while walking around the show this year, presented in no particular order.
  • LiveWire came to EICMA with perhaps its most diverse electric two-wheeler lineup yet, showing just how far the manufacturer has expanded beyond the premium electric motorcycles that originally defined the Harley-Davidson spin-off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that every year, the world’s largest motorcycle companies (and plenty of the world’s smallest motorcycle companies, too) converge on Milan, Italy for Europe’s premier motorcycle showcase. That means that all of the newest electric motorcycle announcements happen in one place, and we get a chance to check out the coolest developments and most interesting new gear.

Below is a list of the best things I saw while walking around the show this year, presented in no particular order.

LiveWire came to EICMA with perhaps its most diverse electric two-wheeler lineup yet, showing just how far the manufacturer has expanded beyond the premium electric motorcycles that originally defined the Harley-Davidson spin-off.

In a recent development, the new S4 Honcho family was a major focus, including the street-oriented Honcho Street, off-road Honcho Trail, and newly unveiled Honcho Skate, a stripped-down addition to the modular platform. The booth also included LiveWire’s larger S2 electric motorcycles, creating a pretty broad spectrum from lightweight urban machines up through full-size highway-capable electric motorcycles.

The other substantial piece of the booth was DUST Moto, which LiveWire acquired earlier this year. The production-intent DUST Hightail was displayed alongside the newly revealed DUST Spur, giving LiveWire an immediate presence in the increasingly popular lightweight electric dirt bike category.

Add in STACYC’s electric balance bikes for young riders, and the entire booth almost looked like an electric two-wheeler progression chart: start a kid on a STACYC, move up through lightweight DUST and Honcho machines, and eventually graduate to a full-size LiveWire.

GR1T Motorcycles is a relatively young European electric motorcycle startup that caught my eye at EICMA with its G1 platform, a lightweight electric motorcycle designed and engineered in Italy. The basic recipe is pretty compelling: 130 km/h (81 mph) top speed, 11 kW of continuous power and 26.6 kW (36 hp) peak, all while weighing just 130 kg (287 lb).

Recent findings suggest that perhaps most importantly for urban riders, its roughly 6 kWh battery is actually split into two removable 3 kWh packs, meaning apartment dwellers can pull the batteries out and charge them inside. They’re big, but removing them is doable.

GR1T’s bikes therefore pack in around 50% more battery capacity than most electric motorcycles in this size and weight class, meaning roughly 50% more range, as well.

There are also some interesting and clever design choices, like the underslung rear suspension and the triple-camera system that includes front and rear dashcams plus a cockpit-facing camera for recording the rider.

Industry observers note that the clever part of the overall design scheme is that GR1T isn’t developing a separate platform for every motorcycle. The same basic G1 chassis, motor, batteries, belt drive, and electronics underpin four versions: the G1S Street, G1X Scrambler, G1XR Raider, and utility-oriented G1M Mission.

Prices are set to start at €8,495 including VAT, putting these squarely in that emerging category of reasonably affordable, lightweight electric motorcycles that have enough speed for real-world commuting without chasing superbike performance.

In a recent development, there’s an important caveat, though: these aren’t production motorcycles yet. GR1T indicates it is right now fundraising, with factory development and pre-orders set to follow after funding closes and first deliveries now targeted for the first half of 2028.

So the bikes aren’t quite ready for primetime yet, but it’s definitely a company to watch.

Real Motors brought one of the more visually striking electric motorcycles to EICMA with Project: ARES, a futuristic electric café racer that the American startup describes as an “Electric Analog” machine – basically an attempt to preserve the raw, mechanical connection of motorcycling while ditching unnecessary screens and gadgetry.

And there’s plenty of performance underneath the sci-fi bodywork: Real Motors lists a 75 kW (100 hp) motor, a 15 kWh battery, a 120 mph (192 km/h) top speed, and an estimated weight of 485 lb (220 kg).

The analog analogy is spot on, with the display probably the simplest and most straightforward I’ve ever seen on an electric motorcycle. There’s also no app, no subscription, and no digital handcuffs. The bike is very much the electric equivalent of a simple ICE bike that just rides, albeit with a much nicer ride.

Unlike many of the futuristic concepts scattered around EICMA, ARES is actually headed toward limited production.

Recent findings suggest that real Motors intends to build just 250 examples in its first LOT 01 production run, with pricing starting at $20,000 and North American deliveries targeted for early 2027. European deliveries are expected after homologation is completed.

The company has also brought former LiveWire CTO Vance Strader onto the project as it makes the difficult transition from a very cool prototype into an actual production motorcycle.

It has been revealed that I actually had the chance to do a spin on the bike, and so I’ll be reporting back on the experience. But you can tell from my smile below that the ride was quite an experience!

Seatylock has been my go-to e-bike lock company for several years now, and I use their locks for my several e-bikes and my wife’s e-bike too.

Now Seatylock has returned with some even more impressive locks. The firm showed off its latest Ultra D28 lock, which is both angle grinder-proof and wide enough to lock the wheel of a motorcycle. It solves the problem of how do you make a lock strong enough for a motorcycle but also small and light enough that you can actually carry it with you, unlike a massive chain lock that usually stays where you park your motorcycle overnight.

In the image below, you can see the shackle next to an exposed section demonstrating the diamond coating that essentially destroys angle grinder discs – even diamond coated discs.

The company also has a slightly smaller version of the same lock designed for bicycles.

Both will absolutely destroy even the toughest angle grinder discs. Sure, eventually someone could cut through them, but it may take a dozen discs and by that point the thief has moved on to an easier target.

At EICMA 2026, Royal Enfield continued expanding its electric motorcycle ambitions with its Flying Flea sub-brand, showcasing the scrambler-style motorcycle alongside its growing lineup of lightweight, retro-inspired electric motorcycles.

There were several interesting colorways and customized designs on display, showcasing the Flying Flea’s stylish design.

The latest models blend Royal Enfield’s classic design heritage with modern electric technology, targeting urban riders and those looking for a fun, approachable electric motorcycle rather than a high-performance machine.

With distinctive styling, compact proportions, and an emphasis on accessible riding, the Flying Flea lineup represents Royal Enfield’s effort to carve out a place in the emerging market for smaller electric motorcycles while maintaining the character that has made its gasoline-powered bikes so popular.

Yamaha revealed off its new NMAX E electric scooter, bringing battery-powered performance to one of the brand’s most recognizable urban scooter families.

Designed as an electric alternative to the popular gasoline-powered NMAX, the fresh model combines familiar sporty styling with a quiet, low-maintenance electric drivetrain aimed at everyday city commuting.

The NMAX E uses Yamaha’s latest compact eAxle powertrain, shared with the larger-wheeled XENTER E, and delivers up to 7.5 kW (10 hp) of peak power, putting it in the 125cc-equivalent class.

With its practical step-through design, automatic operation, and approachable performance, the NMAX E represents another step in Yamaha’s push to electrify its urban mobility lineup, particularly in European markets where scooters are already a popular alternative to cars.

Segway indicated off a newly introduced vision for safer electric scooters, including its futuristic X Cruiser concept that takes rider protection to a whole new level.

Rather than relying solely on traditional motorcycle safety equipment, the X Cruiser explores automotive-inspired features such as integrated seats with seatbelts, partial enclosures, and even a fully roofed version designed to offer additional protection from the elements.

The concept includes several configurations, ranging from a more conventional open scooter to a partially enclosed design and a fully covered model that looks like a cross between a motorcycle and a tiny electric car. While these designs are still concepts rather than production-ready scooters, they demonstrate how Segway is rethinking two-wheeled transportation by exploring ways to make electric scooters safer, more comfortable, and potentially more appealing to riders who might otherwise be hesitant to trade four wheels for two.

Eli Electric Vehicles took to EICMA 2026 to display its compact Eli Zero electric quadricycle, a tiny two-seat urban EV designed to offer much of the convenience of a car without the size, weight, or expense of a conventional automobile.

With its enclosed cabin, side-by-side seating, and ultra-compact footprint, the Eli Zero offers a practical alternative to larger vehicles for short city trips, combining the weather protection and comfort of a car with the maneuverability and efficiency of a much smaller vehicle.

The company revealed a more powerful L7e-class version of the Eli Zero that it had previously teased, expanding the vehicle’s capabilities beyond its existing L6e configuration. The upcoming Race Edition also pushes the envelope farther with custom interior and a few extra accents to the body.

With growing interest in smaller, more efficient urban transportation, Eli’s presence at EICMA definitely underlined how the show is increasingly embracing electric mobility solutions that go beyond traditional motorcycles and scooters.

NIU demonstrated off its latest lineup of electric scooters, continuing the brand’s push to make battery-powered two-wheelers a practical alternative to gasoline-powered urban transportation. Known for its sleek designs, connected technology, and approachable electric scooters, NIU highlighted models aimed at a range of riders, from everyday city commuters to those looking for more powerful machines capable of keeping up with faster urban traffic.

The company revealed off several newly introduced models for the 2027 model year, with scooters that combine modern styling with features such as smartphone connectivity, smart security systems, and efficient electric drivetrains, all while maintaining the simplicity and low operating costs that make electric scooters so appealing.

While I didn’t see anything groundbreaking at the brand’s booth this year, the incremental updates look to push new tech features further throughout the brand’s many models, helping more of NIU’s offerings enter that premium level that the firm has been known for.

For something a bit wilder, Honda shared its futuristic EV Outlier Concept, an electric motorcycle that explores what two-wheeled design could look like when engineers are freed from the constraints of traditional gasoline-powered motorcycles.

With its long, low-slung profile, radically different riding position, and futuristic bodywork, the EV Outlier looks more like something out of a science fiction movie than a conventional motorcycle. The concept features electric motors integrated into both wheels, giving it two-wheel drive while opening up fresh possibilities for packaging and weight distribution.

Rather than simply replacing a combustion engine with a battery and motor, Honda used the EV Outlier to rethink the entire motorcycle layout, demonstrating how electrification could lead to entirely new types of riding experiences.

While the bike remains a design concept with no announced production plans, it offers an intriguing glimpse into Honda’s vision for the future of electric motorcycles.

Sources indicate that vespa showed off its next-generation electric scooter lineup at EICMA, including electric versions of the Primavera, Sprint S, and Primavera Tech. While they don’t look radically different, there’s a lot more happening underneath the familiar steel bodywork.

A latest Italian-made, rare-earth-free electric motor improves efficiency and performance, while the 45 km/h Primavera and Sprint S now feature removable batteries.

The faster 67 km/h Primavera Tech gets up to 90 km of WMTC range – a 12.5% improvement – along with an updated vehicle management system and more efficient charger.

In a recent development, FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More.

Micah Toll is a personal electric vehicle enthusiast, battery nerd, and author of the Amazon #1 bestselling books DIY Lithium Batteries, DIY Solar Power, The Ultimate DIY Ebike Guide and The Electric Bike Manifesto.

The e-bikes that make up Micah’s current daily drivers are the $999 Lectric XP 2.0, the $1,095 Ride1Up Roadster V2, the $1,199 Rad Power Bikes RadMission, and the $3,299 Priority Current. But it’s a pretty evolving list these days.

Industry observers note that “With any vibrator you’re using, you’re going to want to make sure you’re cleaning it after every session,” Richmond explains. A dirty vibrator can hold bacteria and germs—which, needless to say, can seriously kill the mood.

It has been revealed that if you don’t have a sex toy-specific cleanser on hand, you can always use mild soap and warm water to clean your products, claims Mintz. Some toys are even dishwasher-safe. Plus, she notes, they’re easy to use: “You spray them on, leave them to sit, and then wipe them off.” Just make sure your toy is fully dry before you put it away.

Finally, if you have a collection of pleasure products, store them separately, Mintz warns. If you forget to clean one vibrator and then toss it in a bag with several other sex toys, the germs and bacteria can spread to your other products.

Sex-positive, sex toy-specific online stores such as Lovehoney, Babeland, and Good Vibrations are always great places to start, claims Mintz. “I would recommend going to a reputable sex shop that has [customer] reviews,” she says.

Hyundai is skipping the typical mid-cycle refresh and plans to launch a completely redesigned Kona, with a sleek upcoming style and an updated high-tech interior.

It’s been nearly four years since Hyundai introduced the second-generation Kona, meaning, like most of its models, the compact SUV was expected to receive a mid-cycle refresh.

Hyundai is apparently going straight to the third-generation model instead. Earlier this year, early-stage prototypes were spotted in Korea that looked much boxier and more rugged than the current Kona.

Since then, several test mules have been captured testing in the US, Europe, and other regions, confirming the Kona will adopt a more upright, traditional SUV design similar to the latest Santa Fe, Palisade, and Tucson.

The wider, more powerful design appears to draw inspiration from Hyundai’s off-road Crater Concept, revealed at the LA Auto Show last year.

Hyundai noted the off-road SUV Concept was a preview of the “next evolution” of its Extreme Rugged Terrain (XRT) vehicles, such as the IONIQ 5 XRT and Palisade XRT Pro. Is the Kona next in line to receive the XRT treatment?

A post shared by SHORTS CAR (@shorts_car).

Apparent leaked images from a few months ago revealed a design that looked like a mashup of the Crater Concept and IONIQ 5, with pixelated lighting and a clamshell hood.

Sources indicate that most recently, the third-gen Hyundai Kona, codenamed “SX3,” was spotted disguised in a parking garage in Korea. The images were sent to ShortsCar, revealing the new Kona’s wheel design.

Tesla stops selling every Cybertruck except the $109,990 Cyberbeast

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (807 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla is now only selling one version of the Cybertruck in the US: the tri-motor Cyberbeast, which just got another $7,500 price hike to $109,990.
  • It has been revealed that the Dual Motor and Premium AWD trims are still listed on Tesla’s configurator, but both are greyed out and can’t be selected.
  • Here’s what Tesla’s US configurator shows today with a Los Angeles delivery address:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla is now only selling one version of the Cybertruck in the US: the tri-motor Cyberbeast, which just got another $7,500 price hike to $109,990.

It has been revealed that the Dual Motor and Premium AWD trims are still listed on Tesla’s configurator, but both are greyed out and can’t be selected. So the cheapest Cybertruck you can order today costs $109,990, up 57% from $69,990 in early August.

Here’s what Tesla’s US configurator shows today with a Los Angeles delivery address:.

A week ago, the Cyberbeast cost $102,490. Before that, it was $99,990. That’s a $10,000 (10%) increase in about a week on a truck that hasn’t changed: 320 miles of estimated range, 11,000 lbs of towing, and 0-60 mph in 2.6 seconds.

According to recent reports, on November 6, the same day Elon Musk announced the end of Cybertruck production, Tesla raised Cybertruck prices by up to 10% and paused orders for the base Dual Motor. That made the $92,490 Premium AWD the entry point. Now it’s gone too, with no announcement. The configurator just stopped letting you pick it.

Latest inventory isn’t an alternative either. When we checked, Tesla’s inventory search revealed no new Cybertrucks within 200 miles of Los Angeles.

This comes two days after Musk extended Cybertruck production through the end of summer 2027 to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” On Monday, he claimed the order rate “far exceeds” production and that Tesla would “have to return deposits for a lot of people.”.

If there really is a backlog, cutting off the two cheaper trims is one way to cap it before the line shuts down. It also pushes whatever demand is left toward the most expensive, highest-margin version of the truck.

But the sales data doesn’t describe a truck with a demand problem in the other direction. We estimate Tesla delivered 7,000 to 8,000 Cybertrucks in Q3, a pace of about 30,000 a year on a line with more than 125,000 units of installed capacity. And in February, Tesla was offering a dual-motor Cybertruck at $59,990 for “only the next 10 days.”.

That’s $50,000 less than the cheapest Cybertruck you can order today. Nine months later.

Some of those $59,990 buyers are still waiting on delivery dates pushed into 2027. Tesla hasn’t said whether their orders, or any other Dual Motor and Premium orders in the queue, will be built before production ends.

Unlike the thousands of $59k CT orders that may never get manufactured I can guarantee that every high margin $110k CyberBeast order will be delivered before production ends.

According to recent reports, this is the wind-down playbook, and it’s moving faster than I expected. Announce the end, raise prices, pull the cheaper trims, and sell the last trucks in their most expensive form. Tesla is squeezing as much as it can out of every remaining Cybertruck.

I don’t blame Tesla for wanting margin on a program it’s walking away from. But it makes the “order backlog” talk look like what we said it was: an end-of-life rush Tesla created by announcing the end, now being monetized with a $109,990 sticker. Not great for anyone who was told in 2019 that this truck would start at $39,900, or that the tri-motor version would cost $69,900.

If you want a Cybertruck that isn’t a Cyberbeast, you’re now shopping used. And I’d keep an eye on used prices, because a truck that’s going out of production with no cheaper upcoming option could hold its value better than it has over the last two years.

The Man With No Butt

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1879 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I REMEMBER THE first time I became aware of it.
  • Upcoming Coke was a thing people cared about.
  • Sources indicate that I was nine years old.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I REMEMBER THE first time I became aware of it. Or should I say lack of it.

I grew up in the mid '80s. A magical time. MTV actually played music videos. Upcoming Coke was a thing people cared about. And a ginger-headed German teenager named Boris Becker—Boom-Boom, to his millions of fans—became, at age 17, the youngest player ever to win Wimbledon.

Sources indicate that I was nine years old. And obsessed.

Recent findings suggest that while other kids my age were collecting Garbage Pail Kids cards or trying to solve Rubik’s Cubes, I was rewatching VHS recordings of Becker’s matches. I practiced his signature serve motion in front of my bedroom mirror. I begged—actually begged—my parents for the complete Boris Becker starter kit: the Ellesse tennis outfit, the Puma half-top sneakers, and the holy grail itself: the Puma Super tennis racket.

Industry observers note that the problem was, no matter how hard I tried, no matter how much Hi-C I consumed, I could never quite achieve the same explosive spring that made Boom-Boom so spectacular. Then I noticed something about Becker’s serve—the one that earned him his nickname. Most players bent their knees to generate power. Becker did something else.

He stuck out his butt. Like, really stuck it out. His serve motion involved this pronounced posterior thrust that helped him achieve that devastating topspin and pace.

I went to the bedroom mirror. Turned sideways. Attempted the same motion. And that’s when it hit me with all the force of one of Becker’s 130-mph serves: I didn’t have a butt to stick out. Where Becker had curvature, I had...continuity. My back just sort of continued into my legs.

Industry observers note that reality set in. No bum-bum, no boom-boom.

Industry observers note that by high school, I had pivoted to more cerebral pursuits like creative writing and a burgeoning interest in art history. Art history seemed safe—just looking at old paintings and Roman sculptures, right? Wrong. It became immediately clear that every civilization in human history had one thing in common: great asses.

One fateful morning during my sophomore year, I was standing at my locker wearing a pair of saggy-bottomed Gap khakis when I heard giggles behind me. The distinctive sound of teenage girls discovering something hilarious and vaguely cruel.

In a recent development, “Oh my God,” one of them remarked. I froze.

“He has no butt!” another voice announced with the confidence of a scientist making a groundbreaking discovery. More giggling. Then came the death blow that would echo through the halls of my high school for the next two and a half years:.

Sure, it wasn’t the most creative nickname, but it had just enough alliteration to spread like a pre-internet meme. From that day on, I knew “they” knew.

I RECENTLY TURNED 50. I’m happily married and have two amazing kids. Life is good, but I’d be lying if I remarked the ghost of No-Butt Bender doesn’t haunt me. As I’ve aged, what little I had has somehow continued to erode. My wife loves me despite my anatomical deficiency but remains perpetually baffled by the lack of rear topography. And what was once giggles from teenage girls is now full-throated hysterical laughter from my 13- and 11-year-old children when they catch a glimpse of me in anything form-fitting.

Recently, Instagram’s insecurity algorithm served me up an ad for Perk men’s clothing. Their website is a gallery of flattering middle-aged bum-shots, but what really stopped my scroll was the pitch for their pants: “Our chinos magically turn even a flat butt into a compliment magnet. Whether you’re 25 or 65, that never gets old!”.

It has been revealed that you have to understand—when you have no butt, no pants are flattering. So when Perk starts advertising pants that promise to be so bootylicious you’ll receive compliments everywhere you go, I dared to dream. I did what any man starved for posterior validation does—panic-ordered chinos in every damn color.

Five pairs. Overnight shipping.

The moment the package arrived, I tore it open. I slipped them on, turned toward the mirror, and—holy hell—was that…something? An actual curve? A protrusion? I squinted. I turned. And I practically sprinted to the living room where the family was waiting and struck a pose.

Crickets. Then a full collapse into hysterical laughter.

“I’m sorry,” my wife gasped between laughs, “but those pants are working so hard and getting nowhere.”.

Recent findings suggest that I was tired of feeling like the only person other than Hank Hill to be cursed with diminished gluteal syndrome (DGS). It’s a very isolating condition. But I figured if Perk could build an entire company around flat-figured men, there had to be others out there, living their lives in quiet resignation.

Close to midnight on a Wednesday, my face lit only by the glow of my computer, I did the obvious: Googled “men with no butts.”.

Sources indicate that the search results led me to a Reddit post titled, “Gentlemen, how do you live with having no butt?” This guy laid it all out: approaching 29, finally accepting his glute-free reality, enduring constant jokes from his girlfriend, the whole nine yards of tush-less trauma. But what really got me was his closing line: “Please help.”.

I stared at those two words. They contained decades of my own experience—the loneliness, the confusion, the desperation. This post was five years old, but I didn’t care. I had to reach out.

I woke the following morning to find his response waiting like a message from a long-lost brother: “You seem legit I guess. Sure why not.” We were already bonding!

I asked Ross (names have been changed to protect the in-ass-cent) what motivated him to publicly post about his crisis on Reddit, and he said, “It was a genuine problem and if someone’s got an answer that helps, I was going to be all ears.”.

Ross first became aware of his DGS when a friend at the gym dropped the bomb: “Dude, you have no ass whatsoever.” The keen observation sent Ross into a spiral of photographic evidence review. He started examining pictures of himself and came to the only possible conclusion: “Huh, I guess I don’t.” It was his own bedroom-mirror moment.

In a recent development, as for the wisdom he received from the Reddit hivemind, he mentioned it was mostly people prescribing the usual suspects: sprints and squats: “I was doing a shit ton of those back then and still do,” he told me. Five years later, he reports modest gains: “It’s no dump truck but I’ve got a little bit of cushion for comfort back there.” He eventually broke up with the ass-teaser (good riddance) and has been dating a new lady who actually pinches it every now and then—a gesture that, for men like us, feels like winning the Mega Millions.

But the struggle continues. Despite his Stairmaster devotion, sweatpants still “kind of sag” making it look like he may have taken a small dump in them. Still, Ross gave me the faintest glimmer that improvement was possible. Maybe a guy with no butt could transform it into a bona fide ba-donk-a-donk.

I phoned two lifelines from my past—Jonathan Botts, MD, a college friend who’d become an orthopedic surgeon at the Los Angeles Orthopedic Institute in Sherman Oaks, California, and Derek DeGrazio, Britney Spears’s former physical trainer, who had whipped me into the best shape of my life for my long-ago wedding and now is a partner at Barry’s Bootcamp Miami.

It has been revealed that dr. Botts (who inexplicably escaped high school without a single butt-related nickname) broke down the anatomy: the butt consists of three muscles—the gluteus maximus, medius, and minimus—but it’s the maximus that does the heavy lifting in filling out a man’s pants.

Industry observers note that when I asked about the possibility of maximizing my non-existus, he didn’t sugarcoat it. “Here’s the problem: You can’t go from what you are now to just working on your butt and developing a huge butt,” he told me. “People are doing lots of protein intake and protein shakes and bulking up like that. You could get bigger and your butt would get bigger with you. Muscularly. But I don’t know. I don’t think you could take huge leaps with just doing squats and lunges.”.

So basically, I’d need to become the Hulk to grow a butt.

Industry observers note that derek offered an alternate strategy with what he calls the Bender Big Three™. “I can’t say for certain, but I think No-Butt Bender can become Mild-Butt Bender with squats for foundation, Romanian deadlifts to pop your glute a little bit, and a nice hip thrust,” he said.

Mild-Butt Bender. It did have a certain je ne sais quoi.

Derek, who freely admits he was born with “a great Italian ass,” is my gluteal bizarro from an alternate universe where only perfect butts exist. He told me his seat meat gave him confidence in high school, something I could only imagine by taping Springsteen’s Born in the USA album cover to the back of my pants. Derek played baseball, a sport notorious for its revealing tight pants. “I don’t know if they came to watch baseball or if they came to watch us in our uniforms,” he recalled, misty-eyed.

I hated him. I loved him. I wanted to be him.

But then—plot twist!—just as I began fantasizing about playing shortstop, Derek dropped a bomb: “I started to realize that what was a blessing at one point became also my Achilles heel at the same time. If there is a downside, I wasn’t the fastest guy on the team.”.

Industry observers note that wait. There was a downside to having a butt?

Recent findings suggest that dr. Botts, who describes his own posterior as “bigger than average,” delivered the final revelation: Having a bigger butt doesn’t automatically mean you have a stronger butt. “If you have a small butt, does that mean you have weak glutes? It doesn’t at all. You can have a substantial butt and have really weak glutes.”.

All these years, I’d associated my small butt with weakness. With inadequacy. With being less than. What if I was wrong? What if, beneath my perpetually drooping pants lurked a superhero-strength posterior more powerful than even Derek’s celebrated Italian ass?

It has been revealed that unlikely. And who am I kidding? It’s not like if I had said to those girls in high school, “Oh no, you don’t understand—it’s really strong!” they would have stopped laughing and made out with me.

But hey, this latest knowledge gives me something to cling on to. Wish I could say the same for my pants. Still, I am what I am. I am No-Butt Bender. And if that makes my kids laugh and my wife give me a warm, “It’s okay. I love you anyway” hug, I’ll take it.

Latest Update: TikTok’s Viral Winter Arc Challenge Is the Best Way to Get a Jump-Start on Your New Year’s Goals

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (871 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that between holiday parties, happy hours, and meeting your job’s Q4 goals, it may be hard to motivate yourself to lock in on your goals for the remainder of the year.
  • That’s where the 90-day Winter Arc Challenge comes into play.
  • It has been revealed that this time of year tends to be stressful, but the Winter Arc Challenge “helps to keep the stress in perspective and also helps us to not get off track or out of balance with the bigger picture” in terms of your goals, notes Chloe Carmichael, PhD, a clinical psychologist and Women's Health advisory board member based in Newly introduced York City.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that between holiday parties, happy hours, and meeting your job’s Q4 goals, it may be hard to motivate yourself to lock in on your goals for the remainder of the year. While, yes, you should cut yourself some slack here and there during the busy holiday season, it’s also more key now than ever to finish the year strong.

That’s where the 90-day Winter Arc Challenge comes into play. This annual challenge, which originally went viral on TikTok back in 2024, starts October 1 and ends January 1 (but if you missed the start, it’s not too late!). The only premise: Stay locked in on your goals for the rest of the calendar year, whether that’s training for a half-marathon, hitting your Goodreads book quota, or mastering a latest hobby.

It has been revealed that this time of year tends to be stressful, but the Winter Arc Challenge “helps to keep the stress in perspective and also helps us to not get off track or out of balance with the bigger picture” in terms of your goals, notes Chloe Carmichael, PhD, a clinical psychologist and Women's Health advisory board member based in Newly introduced York City. Now’s the time for you to “be intentional about your energy and what serves you.”.

In a recent development, if you haven’t started the challenge yet, it’s not too late. Whether you try it for 83 or 30 days, the Winter Arc Challenge will set you up for greater success with your New Year’s goals because it’ll strengthen your self-efficacy, or “your sense of belief in your own ability to do what you say that you are going to do,” states Carmichael. Self-efficacy is strengthened through your own behavioral track record, so if you start meeting goals now, you’ll already have momentum heading into January, she explains.

Ready to tackle your own Winter Arc Challenge? Here are some helpful tips to help you make the most of the next few months:.

Sources indicate that maybe as part of your Winter Arc Challenge, you aim to cut your monthly spending in half. But a few weeks after setting this goal, you really go overboard at brunches and parties. Don't sweat it. This is “a completely normal part of the change process,” Carmichael says. Instead of giving up when you encounter a relapse here or there, proposal for bumps to happen, then get back on track.

Recent findings suggest that so, if you spend too much money one week, instead of falling into a pattern of negative self-talk, replace your thoughts. Carmichael claims to blueprint a script of what you can say to yourself when you relapse, like: “I can still get back on track and feel good about my goals. This is my moment to restart.”.

Say you’re planning to work out four times a week until the end of the year. If you know the cold morning weather is going to persuade you to stay under the covers and sleep in, be proactive: Book workout classes online every week so you know they’re in your calendar, and you’re more likely to show up. Also, write down your challenges—like the dropping temps preventing you from leaving your house—to keep yourself accountable, Carmichael adds.

Recent findings suggest that picture yourself on January 1 having been successful with your Winter Arc Challenge, then move backward and think about everything that led up to it. If your substantial goal was to do a yoga class every week, visualize yourself walking through the snow to get to your Monday night class, or doing a virtual class at home when there was a bad blizzard. Also think about when you almost skipped classes and fell off the wagon, but you used thought replacements to continue reinforcing your goals. Using imagery will help you mentally prepare for the journey ahead, Carmichael indicates.

Industry observers note that ask around to see if any of your friends are also doing the Winter Arc Challenge—or if they’re willing to hold you accountable. Then, plan regular meetups or calls to check in. “Talk about how things went with a promise to be honest and supportive if one or both of you is falling off,” Carmichael says. “It will help you to stay consistent when you can leverage your social support network.”.

Recent findings suggest that no matter when you started the Winter Arc Challenge, you’ll see and feel the benefits of bettering yourself in no time. Good luck—you got this!

Walking, Yoga, or Zumba? Which Exercises Help Relieve Menopause Mood Symptoms

📅 17 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (751 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Physical activity may help support mood and improve quality of life during the menopause transition, according to a study published on October 13 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society.
  • This review of 12 clinical trials involving over 1,000 people ages 40 to 65 found that both aerobic and mind-body exercises may be associated with reduced depressive symptoms and improved well-being.
  • It is common for individuals to experience psychological symptoms during menopause, including depression, anxiety, low mood, stress, and difficulty with thinking and memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Physical activity may help support mood and improve quality of life during the menopause transition, according to a study published on October 13 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society.

This review of 12 clinical trials involving over 1,000 people ages 40 to 65 found that both aerobic and mind-body exercises may be associated with reduced depressive symptoms and improved well-being.

It is common for individuals to experience psychological symptoms during menopause, including depression, anxiety, low mood, stress, and difficulty with thinking and memory. These symptoms can have a significant effect on quality of life, with an estimated 1 in 10 women leaving work due to menopause symptoms.

This study found that regular physical activity may help improve certain psychological symptoms and overall quality of life during menopause.

The types of physical activity in the review were broken into two categories: aerobic-based exercise (ABIs) and mind-body activities (MBAs).

Industry observers note that the researchers found that ABIs showed the strongest effects on reducing depressive symptoms and improving overall quality of life. This may be particularly relevant during perimenopause when women may be more vulnerable to mood instability due to estrogen fluctuations.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, pointed out that there are various ways that ABIs can have positive effects.

Ross explained that aerobic exercise may help improve menopausal symptoms through several mechanisms, including the release of endorphins, reduced inflammation, improved cholesterol levels, and better regulation of body temperature and sleep cycles.

Recent findings suggest that MBAs were shown to have a greater effect on improving psychological quality of life. These exercises involve mindfulness, body awareness, and breathwork. They may help improve emotional regulation.

It has been revealed that ABIs tended to require fewer sessions. This may mean these types of exercises are easier to fit in, especially if you are facing time or energy constraints. For example, in one trial, participants were instructed to walk for 30 minutes, three times per week. In another trial, participants attended three hour-long Zumba classes per week.

In contrast, one trial using MBAs instructed participants to attend two 75-minute yoga classes each week, and another had participants attend daily one-hour yoga classes.

Stephanie Faubion, MD, Director for the Mayo Clinic Center for Women’s Health and Medical Director for The Menopause Society, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are encouraging.

Recent findings suggest that however, she also cautioned that this was a relatively small body of evidence. “While physical activity is an important component of a healthy lifestyle during midlife, I would be cautious about interpreting these findings to mean that exercise is a treatment for depression related specifically to menopause,” she remarked.

Research has shown that physical activity can positively affect mental health. Studies have also found that regular exercise can help improve symptoms of depression and anxiety.

Faubion told Healthline that, broadly speaking, regular physical activity may support mood through multiple pathways, including better sleep, improved physical function, and overall well-being.

However, she also noted that this study cannot tell us precisely why the improvements occurred or whether aerobic exercise is superior to other forms of activity.

Faubion noted that recommending physical activity during and after menopause extends well beyond mood.

“Physical activity is important for cardiovascular and metabolic health, maintaining muscle mass and physical function, and supporting bone health,” she said.

“These become particularly important at midlife as women experience age- and menopause-related changes in body composition, bone, and cardiometabolic health,” Faubion added.

Sources indicate that ross agreed that physical activity is important for more than just mood and mental health improvement. She also noted that there are other types of exercise beyond ABIs and MBAs that can benefit people during menopause:.

“These types of activities help with weight loss or allow women to maintain a healthy weight. If you are not ready for aerobic exercises, stretching and simple exercises help with balance and stability,” Ross said.

Faubion told Healthline that physical activity is an important part of healthy aging and should be encouraged during the menopause transition, but it should not be suggested that women can simply exercise their way out of significant depression or other bothersome menopause symptoms.

“Women experiencing persistent depression, anxiety, or symptoms that interfere with their quality of life should seek evaluation and discuss the full range of evidence-based treatment options with their healthcare clinician,” Faubion said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that I’M A SUCKER for a good Barbour jacket. I’ve always considered the British heritage brand’s waxed-cotton outerwear the perfect finishing touch to a nicely put-together fall-winter outfit. Founded in 1894, Barbour originally made weather-resistant jackets for sailors, fishermen, and outdoor workers before becoming a staple of British countryside dressing. Over the years, its association with the royal family, including Princess Diana and King Charles III, helped give the rugged outerwear an upper-class appeal. But in the past five years, Barbour has seen a major resurgence, thanks to the barn-jacket boom on runways at Prada, Loewe, and Bottega Veneta, along with a growing appetite for timeless pieces over fast fashion. Buzzy collaborations with designers like Gucci and Paul Smith, plus the popularity of British countryside style in shows like The Crown, have also introduced the look to a whole latest generation of guys.

But as much as I love Barbour jackets, dropping several hundred dollars on one isn’t exactly in everyone’s budget. Some of the brand’s most iconic styles, including the Bedale, Beaufort, and Ashby, will set you back anywhere from $415 to $450. And that’s before you dive into the designer collabs. Take the latest J.Crew x Barbour Beaufort jacket. It’s a fresh, reimagined take on the brand’s signature outerwear, dressed in a bold apple-green shade with a weather-resistant finish and tartan lining. Personally, it has me in a chokehold. At nearly $500, it’s a pretty steep investment, especially if you’re just looking to dip your toes into the barn-jacket trend.

Thankfully, you don’t have to spend that kind of money to capture the same British countryside charm. Plenty of menswear brands have put their own spin on the classic barn jacket, offering similar silhouettes, canvas fabrics, and utilitarian details at more digestible prices. I’ve rounded up some stylish Barbour jacket alternatives from brands like Bonobos and Quince that look just as sharp, whether you’re getting dressed up or keeping it casual.

Recent findings suggest that of all the Barbour jacket alternatives I’ve tested, Quince’s version comes close in comparison to the Barbour x Paul Smith collaboration I already own. That jacket runs north of $800, while Quince’s costs just over a hundred bucks but with nearly all the same bells and whistles: a two-tone brown colorway, contrasting corduroy collar, and snap-button storm throat flap that helps seal out drafts of wind. There’s also a two-way zipper that lets me open the jacket from the bottom when I need a little more breathing room.

It’s made from 100% organic cotton and fully lined with soft cotton flannel, which adds a welcome layer of warmth on chilly days when I can skip wearing a bulky sweater underneath. The cut hits just below the waist, with a roomy fit that leaves plenty of space for layering without feeling overly baggy. I’ve even worn it through a few light rain showers, and the fabric didn’t get soaked. I also appreciate how the classic design makes it easy to dress up with trousers and an Oxford shirt or keep things casual with jeans and boots.

Uniqlo makes one of the best affordable Barbour alternatives I’ve come across, and at just $80, it looks and feels more expensive than it actually is. The lightly padded cotton-nylon fabric provides just enough warmth for temps below 60 degrees. What I especially like is the clean, sleek design that comes with a concealed front closure that hides the buttons and zipper, giving the jacket a sharper, more polished look when fully fastened. There’s also a classic checked lining and two-way flap pockets that can be accessed from the top or sides.

In a recent development, fit-wise, it has a relaxed, boxy silhouette that hits right at the waist and leaves enough room to comfortably layer a chunky knit over a dress shirt. And unlike some barn jackets that lean heavily into the rugged workwear aesthetic, this one feels a little more understated. It comes in versatile neutrals like olive, khaki, black, and dark brown, so finding one that works with your wardrobe shouldn’t be difficult.

Industry observers note that if you’re looking for something that puts a slightly different spin on the traditional barn jacket, Bonobos has you covered. Its Canvas Ranch Jacket trades the usual waxed-cotton construction for a sturdy cotton-elastane blend that has a little stretch, so I’m not feeling boxed in. But what really caught my attention are the angled patch pockets across the front. They’re a subtle departure from the usual straight-cut or flap pockets you see on most field jackets, giving the whole design a more distinctive, modern feel.

The cut extends past the waist and lands around the upper thigh, offering a little more coverage than your typical trucker jacket. I also like that Bonobos keeps the color options simple with midnight navy and forest green, both of which go nicely with denim, chinos, or tailored trousers.

For guys who want the classic Barbour look with a little more protection against the elements, consider this insulated version from L.L.Bean. Unlike some of the lighter options on this list, this one is packed with 60 grams of PrimaLoft Black insulation, a lightweight synthetic fill that helps keep it toasty inside without the bulk of a heavy winter coat. The 100% cotton exterior has a water-resistant waxed finish that will keep you dry in light rain. It also has a quilted exterior that gives the traditional field-jacket silhouette a slightly more outdoorsy vibe.

It’s slightly fitted, so guys who are super jacked might have to size up. But the regular-length cut makes it easy to wear over everyday layers and not feel overly snug. This is a great option for construction laborers, landscapers, and other guys who spend long hours outdoors. It’s more practical than fashion-forward, but you get the timeless look of a heritage field jacket with added insulation and weather protection that make it useful beyond just completing an outfit.

It has been revealed that flint and Tinder’s waxed trucker jacket famously appeared on Pedro Pascal in HBO’s The Last of Us, and we’ve been major fans ever since. This is a burly, no-nonsense trucker jacket made from Martexin waxed sailcloth that’s treated on both sides to help block wind and repel light rain. The antique-finish metal buttons and earthy color options give it that rugged, worn-in look that only gets better with age. On the inside, a full-length blanket-style lining keeps you cozy during 50-degree mornings.

One thing worth mentioning is that the waxed fabric feels pretty stiff at first, so don’t expect it to have that soft, broken-in feel right out of the gate. But that’s also part of the appeal of this type of outerwear. After three wears, the fabric gradually softens and develops more character. Compared to Barbour’s longer field jackets, this one has a more traditional trucker silhouette, so I can pair it with jeans, boots, and other casual staples.

Not every Barbour alternative needs to look like it belongs in the English countryside. Case in point: AYR’s The Club, which takes a more refined approach. It’s made from weatherproofed waxed cotton that offers a water-repellent finish. The fabric is also light enough to wear across three seasons, making it a versatile option for those in-between days when a heavy coat feels like overkill.

I can throw it over a tee with jeans for the weekend or wear it with a collared shirt and trousers to the office. I wore it in light showers, and it didn’t soak through to my clothes. And at a little over $300, it’s certainly not the cheapest alternative on this list. Still, if you’re after something that feels more stylish than rugged, this one makes a strong case for itself.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

In a recent development, there are so many reasons to watch sports, from the obvious excitement that comes with game day to joining a built-in community of fans. But now, upcoming research suggests it may also be linked to fewer symptoms of depression for one group of adults.

The study focused on people with congenital heart disease (which is a range of structural abnormalities of the heart that someone is born with; an estimated 1.4 million adults in the U.S. live with the condition). But the findings are also in line with many other health benefits of watching sports, experts point out.

While many forms of congenital heart disease can be treated, symptoms of depression are more common in this group compared to others without the disease. The upcoming study found a clear link between sports fans with congenital heart disease and those with the disease who didn't watch sports. The findings don't suggest that people should skip proven treatment options for depression in favor of watching games, but they do hint that having a sports-watching habit could give some patients an edge in the mental health department.

It has been revealed that experts also say watching sports is linked to many positive health outcomes—not just for those with congenital heart disease. Here’s what they say.

Meet the experts: Thea Gallagher, PsyD, clinical associate professor at NYU Langone Health and co-host of the Mind in View podcast; Jason Andrus, MD, chair of psychiatry, Northwell’s Northern Westchester Hospital; and Navjot Kaur Sobti, MD, interventional cardiologist and women’s health expert, Northwell’s Northern Westchester Hospital.

The study, which was published in the European Journal of Cardiovascular Nursing, recruited 108 adults with congenital heart disease and asked them whether they watched sports and how often. Researchers also gave participants a standardized questionnaire to look for symptoms of depression.

In a recent development, the researchers found that participants who attended a sports game in person at least once in the previous year had fewer symptoms of depression than those who didn't attend any sporting events. But those who watched sports on TV or online at least once a week also had fewer symptoms of depression compared to those who didn't watch sports.

The study didn't prove that watching sports actually lowered the risk of depression—instead, it found a link between people watching sports and fewer symptoms of depression. Still, doctors say there's likely something here.

"One possible explanation is that sports offer connection, enjoyment, and something to look forward to," notes Thea Gallagher, PsyD, clinical associate professor at NYU Langone Health and co-host of the Mind in View podcast. "Following a team can give people a shared identity and an easy reason to call a friend, get together, or feel part of a larger community.".

Recent findings suggest that for people with regular medical appointments or physical limitations, it can also provide them with an interest and identity beyond being a patient, Gallagher says. "From a behavioral perspective, depression often pulls people away from rewarding activities, which can deepen isolation and low mood," she says. "Watching a sport you enjoy could be an accessible way to reconnect with pleasure and other people.".

Watching sports "doesn't replace staying physically active, but it’s a great, socially-connected way to enjoy some downtime," notes Jason Andrus, MD, chair of psychiatry, Northwell’s Northern Westchester Hospital. "A loss of pleasure can be a major factor in depression and perhaps the thrills of victory, or even the agonies of defeat, experienced vicariously while spectating sports, can help break out of the 'blahs' zone," he adds.

People with depression often struggle with low energy, feelings of hopelessness, and trouble concentrating—and that can interfere with taking medications consistently, attending appointments, and maintaining routines around sleep and physical activity, Gallagher states. "Depression can also cause people to withdraw from relationships that provide emotional and practical support, just when they may need that support most," she adds.

Industry observers note that the relationship between congenital heart disease and depression can go both ways, Gallagher states. "Living with a lifelong heart condition, medical uncertainty, and physical limitations can contribute to depression," she points out.

That's why cardiologists have depression on their minds, too. "We routinely screen our patients for depression as well as other mental health conditions as part of holistic and effective cardiac care," notes Navjot Kaur Sobti, MD, interventional cardiologist and women’s health expert, Northwell’s Northern Westchester Hospital.

It makes sense that playing sports could have serious benefits for cardiovascular health, strength training, community-building, and boosting longevity...but experts point out that anyone can reap the social and health benefits that come with spectating. "The strongest case is for psychological and social benefits," Gallagher says. She notes that people who attend live sports events often feel less lonely and have a greater sense that life is worthwhile.

"Watching sports can also create opportunities for shared enjoyment, conversation, and belonging, although the experience will depend on the person and how they engage with it," she claims.

Overall, Gallagher says the findings are a reminder to ask people what they enjoy and what helps them to feel connected. "For someone who loves sports, following a team may be an accessible way to keep those experiences in their life, particularly when illness makes other activities harder," she says.

Sources indicate that carina Hsieh, MPH, is the deputy features editor of Women’s Health. She has more than a decade’s worth of experience working in media and has covered everything from beauty, fashion, travel, lifestyle, pets, to health.

She began her career as an intern in the fashion closet at Cosmopolitan where she worked her way up to Senior Sex & Relationships Editor. While covering women’s health there, she discovered her passion for health service journalism and took a break to get her Masters in Public Health. Post-grad school, she worked as a freelance writer and as The Daily Beast’s first Beauty, Health, and Wellness Reporter.

In a recent development, carina is an alum of the Fashion Institute of Technology and the Yale School of Public Health. She and her French Bulldog, Bao Bao, split their time between Brooklyn and Connecticut. She enjoys reformer Pilates, (slow) running, and smelling the fancy toiletries in boutique fitness class locker rooms.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After delaying development of the long-awaited electric Golf, Volkswagen is delaying another EV based on its SSP platform.
  • As it scrambles to cut costs, Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer revealed in an internal memo at the end of October that development of the all-electric Golf is being delayed at its Wolfsburg plant in Germany.
  • The news comes after the VW Group posted an operating loss of €5.9 billion ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter, its largest quarterly loss since the infamous Dieselgate scandal in 2015.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After delaying development of the long-awaited electric Golf, Volkswagen is delaying another EV based on its SSP platform.

As it scrambles to cut costs, Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer revealed in an internal memo at the end of October that development of the all-electric Golf is being delayed at its Wolfsburg plant in Germany.

The news comes after the VW Group posted an operating loss of €5.9 billion ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter, its largest quarterly loss since the infamous Dieselgate scandal in 2015.

According to recent reports, “We simply can’t afford this work right now,” Schäfer said in the memo reviewed by Reuters. The Wolfsburg plant, AKA the “heart of the VW brand,” is about €300 million ($334.5 million) short of its cost-cutting targets, the memo said.

Volkswagen initially planned to launch the Golf EV in 2028, but Schäfer revealed earlier this year that the long-awaited electric car was delayed until closer to 2030.

Schäfer suggested the delay was because the SSP (Scalable Systems Platform), which is being developed through its partnership with Rivian, was taking longer than expected, again due to costs.

According to Autocar, Volkswagen is now delaying the Audi A4 E-tron as well, another vehicle that was initially planned to be among the first based on the SSP platform.

Industry observers note that production of the electric A4 is being pushed back until at least 2029, a year later than originally planned. While the delay is disappointing for Audi fans (including myself) still waiting for an electric A4, it also puts Audi behind rival luxury brands in the mid-size sedan segment.

BMW has the new i3, and Mercedes-Benz has the C-Class EV, both of which feature major improvements in range, charging, and efficiency over their previous-generation EVs.

Volkswagen noted in 2023 that the 800V SSP will serve as a “single future backbone with integrated electric and electronics architecture,” claiming that more than 40 million models were expected to be built on it.

The manufacturer also stated investment and R&D costs were expected to be reduced by about 30% compared to the current MEB platform, enabling most models “to achieve the same margin compared to their conventionally powered counterparts.”.

Volkswagen’s software struggles started in its internal division, Cariad, leading to delays, missed targets, and budget overruns.

To fix it, VW turned to Rivian, forming a joint venture to develop its next-gen software-defined vehicle (SDV) electrical architecture.

In March, VW stated several test vehicles, including the ID.EVERY1, Audi, and Scout with the SDV architecture underwent “comprehensive evaluation,” and successfully validated over-the-air (OTA) functionality.

Being cash efficient is good, but delays to the next-gen platform that will keep you competitive with rival brands seem like a problem.

It has been revealed that however, the Audi A4 E-tron delay is not entirely about software. The Autocar report claims Audi demanded significant changes to the SSP platform for the A4 E-tron so it more closely matched the current gas version.

Audi reportedly wanted individual footwells for front and rear passengers, which would require repositioning the battery.

The luxury brand also reportedly asked for a 48V electrical system instead of the traditional 12V setup initially planned.

While development of the Golf EV is on hold, VW’s works council said the pause will not delay its launch, promising to make up for lost time. It’s still expected to launch in 2030. The Audi A4 E-tron is now expected to arrive around 2029.

Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Increase Dementia, Stroke Risk

📅 18 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (845 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.
  • UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations.
  • UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.

UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations. This category of foods includes packaged snack foods, sugary cereals, soft drinks, and frozen ready-to-eat meals.

UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

Previous research has linked these foods to adverse cardiometabolic outcomes. This fresh study adds to growing evidence linking high UPF intake to adverse health outcomes.

Industry observers note that this was a cross-sectional analysis of 8,783 adults between the ages of 35 and 69 without cardiovascular disease. The participants were all enrolled in the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Minds (CAHHM) and Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology-MIND (PURE-MIND) cohorts.

The researchers used MRI scans to evaluate the participants’ brains. They also set out to analyze the cross-sectional relationship between UPF consumption, body fat, vascular brain injury (VBI), and cognitive performance.

According to recent reports, they measured the participants’ habitual UPF intake using a food frequency questionnaire. Intake was expressed as servings based on a 2,000-calorie-per-day diet.

It has been revealed that UPFs accounted for an average of 25% of participants’ daily diets. For the individuals with the highest intake, this increased to 45% of everything on their plates, compared to 16% for those who ate the least.

The researchers also noted that UPFs were not just an added part of individual diets. These foods appeared to replace whole foods.

According to recent reports, among people with the highest UPF intake, fruits, vegetables, grains, and other minimally processed foods accounted for 41% of their daily food intake. Among those with the lowest UPF intake, minimally processed foods made up 68% of their daily intake.

It has been revealed that when the researchers compared the highest intake to the lowest, they found that those with a higher intake of UPFs had 1.7% more body fat. They also found that people with a higher UPF intake had higher odds of VBI.

“These findings are concerning, but it is key to remember that an association does not prove cause and effect,” stated Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“From my perspective as a preventive cardiology dietitian, these findings reinforce the importance of nourishing our blood vessels to support both cardiovascular and brain health.”.

Although researchers found no significant differences in cognitive performance, the signs of vascular brain injury observed in the study have been associated with an increased risk of stroke and cognitive decline.

It has been revealed that these findings suggest a possible link between UPF intake and signs of brain changes. However, participants were only assessed once and weren’t followed over time. This means the researchers were unable to determine whether UPFs directly caused the changes.

“While we can’t conclude from this study that limiting UPFs would improve brain health, we have decades of literature demonstrating that higher intakes of green leafy vegetables, brightly colored fruits, whole grains, and lean protein sources are good for brain health,” stated Suzanne Judd, PhD, Director of the UC College of Medicine’s Center for Public Health, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“So focusing more on what can be brought into the diet rather than what should be eliminated might be a good way to start,” she added.

The preservatives [in UPFs] may have a direct impact on the vascular system, while the loss of antioxidants results in a less robust response to inflammation in the body.

“Additionally, sugar or salt is often added to make the food a bit tastier so people consume it in higher quantities. Over-consumption of food can lead to weight gain and diabetes, which can negatively impact brain health,” Judd said.

Judd told Healthline that it is virtually impossible to completely avoid UPFs. Even some “health” foods, like protein powder and some yogurts, are considered ultra-processed.

It is more important to look at diet overall and emphasize consuming foods as close to their natural state as possible, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, and meats purchased raw or frozen and then cooked at home.

Routhenstein recommended starting simply with one manageable swap rather than trying to overhaul your entire diet.

Industry observers note that she said that you should identify an ultra-processed food you eat regularly and consider a more nutrient-rich alternative. It is notable to account for convenience, food preferences, budget, and lifestyle so that the change feels realistic and is sustainable over the long term.

“I want people to feel empowered, not fearful, when making food choices,” said Routhenstein. “Healthy eating does not mean having to cook everything from scratch. What matters most is building consistent, nourishing habits that support both heart and brain health.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

OUR FITNESS EDITORS love to slip on cushy sneakers like the Hoka Clifton 11 for our 5Ks and hot girl walks. But on days when we're lifting heavy, doing a functional strength training workout, or have a gym sesh that switches between lifts and sprints, we turn to our favorite cross-training shoes. If you’re unfamiliar with the term, cross-training is combining different exercise modalities—like cardio, resistance training, and plyometric (rapid movements)—during a gym session. Think of these sneakers as multipurpose powerhouses. They keep your feet locked in, whether you’re deadlifting or speed walking on an under-desk treadmill.

“They’re designed to handle side-to-side movement, quick pivots, and changes in direction—not just forward motion,” says Melissa Lockwood, DPM, a podiatrist at Heartland Foot and Ankle Associates in Bloomington, Illinois. “This makes them more supportive for gym workouts, classes, or sports where your foot needs stability in multiple planes, like pickleball or tennis.” On the flip side, a walking or running shoe usually only supports you in straight-line motion, Lockwood says.

According to recent reports, wearing running sneakers for strength training workouts is generally a no-no (except for the caveat about the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 below). All the podiatrists I spoke with say it’s safer and beneficial to invest in cross-training shoes. That’s because they usually have flatter outsoles and thinner midsoles than running shoes to keep your feet locked in, says Richard H. Graves, DPM, a podiatrist at Sol Foot & Ankle Centers in Long Beach, California. That way, you won’t wobble during your deadlifts and box jumps. The material of cross-training shoes is also more durable than running shoes to resist wear and tear, and has thick heel counters to help prevent ankle injuries.

Whether you're a seasoned weightlifting junkie or a runner on a mission to integrate more training modalities into your routine, read on for the best cross-training shoes you can find.

It has been revealed that after testing dozens of cross-training shoes this past year, the latest lululemon Chargefeel 3 stands out for its impeccable support and stability during speedy, lateral movements like ice skaters, kettlebell squats, and Zumba workouts. We’ve been fans of the Chargefeel line for years, with the previous edition—the Chargefeel 2—winning the best cross-training shoe for our 2025 WH Sneaker Awards. Lululemon has since made a few tweaks that make it even better. “Despite the fact that sneaker fit and feel is extremely subjective, everyone I know who has worked out in the Chargefeel—myself included—has loved its perfect balance of stability and flexibility,” indicates WH executive health and fitness director Jacqueline Andriakos, NASM-CPT.

It’s now 8 ounces instead of 9.1 ounces, and has a lower heel-to-toe drop—6 mm compared to 9.5 mm—to help alleviate stress on the ankles and feet. WH associate style and commerce editor Shannen Zitz loves the wider build for lifting and squatting. She indicates her feet feel locked in and extra secure. “My feet stay securely in place thanks to a forefoot-hugging band on the inside of the shoe and a tough plastic heel counter,” says Zitz. She also notes that the springy EVA foam cushioning makes it a workhorse for walking and running.

Recent findings suggest that and post-workout, it’s a great leisure kick for traveling or running errands. “I recently wore these while traveling, and they kept my feet super happy power walking through the airport and standing on long security and customs lines,” Zitz adds. Andriakos agrees, stating, “The stylish silhouette looks good outside the gym.”.

According to recent reports, the fit is true to size, and the breathable knit upper doesn’t feel constricting when wearing thick socks (perfect for combating blisters!). Although wide size options are not available, the toes still have adequate room to spread with each step or lift. However, Zitz notes the wide outsole may feel too bulky during quick and dynamic HIIT workouts.

Read More: Every Lululemon Shoe, Ranked.

Recent findings suggest that we wouldn’t recommend most running shoes for cross-training, but the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 is an exception. You can effortlessly transition from long runs to deadlifts, thanks to its balanced cushioning and moderate heel-to-toe drop.

In a recent development, compared to the GTS 24, the latest version has slightly softer cushioning, with about 3 mm more foam in the forefoot and 1 mm in the heel, giving it a smoother, more comfortable feel underfoot. It also drops from 12 mm to 10 mm, creating a slightly more level feel. That can make it feel more stable during strength work than higher-drop running shoes.

Sources indicate that at 9 ounces, it’s a lightweight gem, especially for those with overpronation or flat feet during agility drills. Its GuideRails technology—firm foam on both sides of the foot—keeps feet aligned during everything from Bulgarian split squats to lunges to speed walking. Plus, stiff heel padding keeps feet from sliding."These feel super comfortable and supportive for everyday life, traditional workouts, walks, easy runs—you name it," says Melissa Kendter, CPT, a functional strength coach. "I love that this shoe feels well cushioned but doesn't have a huge chunky sole, making it more appropriate for strength workouts than most running shoes.".

Because the outsole is relatively smooth (it’s built for road miles, not side-to-side gym moves), we’d stick to non-slip floors for quick lateral work. If your workouts are heavy on lifting or plyometrics, a flatter cross-trainer like the Nike Metcon 10 may feel steadier and more secure underfoot.

Read More: Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 Review.

We’ve been fans of the Nano series since 2018, and every year we notice Reebok levels up its cushioning and heel stability to keep our feet locked in and comfortable during even the most intense workouts. The midsole padding is firm for balancing during heavy lifts and lateral movements, yet is still bouncy for excellent rebound during HIIT workouts and explosive jumps. The mesh material upper is also firm, keeping you steady when lifting heavy.

MH digital designer Taryn Colbert used to prefer flat lifestyle shoes like Converse or Vans, but has since switched over to the Nano X5 for her cross-training sessions. The stiffer soles offer her better balance, while she notes that the heel counter is dense, meaning it doesn’t flex easily. However, the 7 mm heel-to-toe drop may be too steep for some weightlifters who prefer a ground-feel shoe. But it’s a pro if you like extra heel support.

Industry observers note that the grippy outsole delivers superior traction when executing deadlifts or weighted squats, while the snug laces never budge. Colbert also notes that the breathable material helps combat sweaty feet. Just note that the fit runs tight (consider ordering at least a half-size up), and it weighs 12.1 ounces, making it one of the heaviest shoes in this guide.

If your workouts focus on dynamic moves like kettlebell swings or heavy lifting, the Nobull Drive is a gem. It’s crafted with a breathable mesh knit upper that feels sock-like and keeps feet cool during grueling reps.

The balance of flexibility and firmness makes it simple to transition from the squat rack to the HIIT studio. WH associate editor Olivia Luppino wears them during physical therapy to help maintain balance when doing Bosu ball squats, and then hits the gym to do deadlifts. She also notes the mesh isn’t scratchy—an glitch she has had when wearing this material.

The subtle foam feels similar to a minimally-cushioned running shoe, while the low 4 mm drop keeps Luppino grounded when deadlifting. She also notes that a firm heel counter makes her feet feel secure without too much stiffness. And at 8.3 ounces, it’s the lightest shoe in this guide, which makes it an optimal choice for sprints and mixed-modality workouts.

Nike’s latest Metcon 10 is a top pick among our editors when it comes to pumping iron. Its main update compared to the last iteration is a smaller, stiffer plate strategically placed under the heel to help stabilize the feet when squatting heavy reps or doing deadlifts. Heel-to-toe drop refers to the height difference between the heel and the forefoot of the shoe.

How to Lose Your Love Handles

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
